::: {.callout-note}
## Scoped, not yet run
:::

## The question

@Yavorsky_2021 shows that the match-value standard deviation — the post-search
spread, $\tilde\sigma$ here — can be estimated rather than normalized to one,
given an exogenous search-cost shifter, and that the normalization does real
damage: he estimates 8.16, and fixing it to one reverses the sign of the urban
search-cost coefficient and understates a counterfactual by a factor of three to
four.

He has the shifter (driving distance) but no panel. @Morozov_2021 has the panel
but normalizes the spread. SIFT has both, plus a designed product page that
fixes part of the spread rather than inferring it.

**Ask:** across a grid of true $\tilde\sigma$, what is the bias in search costs,
in preferences, and in a friction counterfactual, when $\tilde\sigma$ is fixed to
one instead of estimated? And how much does the panel reduce the variance of
$\hat{\tilde\sigma}$ relative to a single spell per respondent?

## Design

1. Simulate SIFT data at $\tilde\sigma \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$, spanning the
   normalized value and Yavorsky's field estimate.
2. Fit twice: $\tilde\sigma$ free, and $\tilde\sigma \equiv 1$.
3. Report bias in $\gamma_0$, $\gamma_p$, $\boldsymbol\beta$, $\boldsymbol\kappa$,
   and in a counterfactual that halves search costs.
4. Repeat with $T=1$ to isolate what the panel contributes over and above the
   shifter.

The $T=1$ arm is the interesting one, because it is the closest simulated
analogue of @Yavorsky_2021's own design and lets us say what SIFT adds rather
than merely that SIFT works.

## Expected obstacle

$\gamma_0$ and $\log\tilde\sigma$ lie on a ridge — @Yavorsky_2021 reports a
correlation of 0.95 between them even with 6,511 consumers. Expect the
$\tilde\sigma$-free arm to be imprecise, and report the ridge explicitly rather
than hiding it in a standard error.
